kinds.label: Natural
kinds.desc: Magic as the hidden virtues of things: stones, plants, animals, sympathy and antipathy, worked without spirits.

kinds.label: Celestial and image
kinds.desc: Magic through the stars: images, talismans and seals made at the right hour to draw down a planet's power.

kinds.label: Spirit and daimonic
kinds.desc: Magic through spirits: daimones, angels, demons or the dead, called, bound, served or worshipped.

kinds.label: Words, names and letters
kinds.desc: Magic through speech: charms, spells, divine names, mantras, letters and their numbers.

kinds.label: Divination
kinds.desc: Knowing the hidden or the future: oracles, omens, lots, astrology and the -mancies.

kinds.label: Demonology and the witch
kinds.desc: Magic as a pact with the devil: witches, their crimes and their trials, argued for or against.

kinds.label: Mathematical
kinds.desc: Wonders made by number, figure and machine: magic numbers and squares, automata, mathematical magic.

kinds.label: Mind and will
kinds.desc: Magic as the power of mind: imagination, will, suggestion, mesmerism, New Thought and the law of attraction.

notes.E. B. notes.Arbatel: On the Magic of the Ancients (A: Waite (1898) knew no Arbatel manuscript before the late sixteenth century, took the 1575 Basel print as its first appearance, and found it unconnected to the Keys of Solomon and 'permeated with Christian ideas'. ([p. 49](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69c896426c6f3cc53c85c4ea?page=49))
notes.Johann Weyer, On the Tricks of Demons (D: Weyer, Agrippa's pupil, rejected the Fourth Book as an 'abominable little book' wrongly attributed to Agrippa, and judged books ascribed to Raziel and Raphael to be recent forgeries full of unknown names and seals. ([p. 163](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695925acaecc3a7338f964dc?page=163))
notes.Pseudo-Agrippa, Fourth Book of Occult Ph: Weyer called the Fourth Book an 'abominable little book' falsely fathered on Agrippa by a wicked man, and treated similar books under other names as recent forgeries. ([p. 163](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695925acaecc3a7338f964dc?page=163))
notes.Gabriel Naudé, Apology for Great Men Acc: Naudé (1625) thought it 'a strange thing' that Delrio, Le Loyer, Bodin, de Lancre and Godelmann wrote so passionately on demons and sorcerers as 'never to reject any Story, though ever so fabulous'. ([p. 328](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699201577c226bdd25f98855?page=328))
notes.Nicolas Bergasse, Considérations sur le: Bergasse argues that universal magnetism is a real agent that produces sensation only in a sick organised body, so only the sick can serve as experimental proof of it. ([p. 115](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6991bd4570254d38471e3940?page=115))
notes.Francis Barrett, The Magus, or Celestial: Barrett's Magus (1801) presents natural magic as a real, comprehensive knowledge of Nature that searches out her occult operations and the virtues of metals, stones, plants and animals. ([p. 41](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69593225b91a6184ea943475?page=41))
notes.Karl von Reichenbach, Researches on Magn: Reichenbach holds that a new force, which he names 'Odyle', exists distinct from magnetism, electricity and chemical attraction, and he reserves 'magnetism' for the iron-attracting force. ([p. 221](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6991bd5c70254d38471e4d76?page=221))
notes.James Esdaile, Mesmerism in India|||Mode: Esdaile reports eight months of mesmeric practice in Bengal and claims that painless surgical operations are 'the natural birthright' of the Natives of Bengal. ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6991bd5a70254d38471e4cf2?page=21))
notes.Lewis Spence, An Encyclopaedia of Occult: Spence's Encyclopaedia (1920) says the early church came to regard magic as foreign to its religion, citing the thirty-sixth canon of the Council of Laodicea (364) as an instance. ([p. 303](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6953c85b77f38f6761bdc00b?page=303))
notes.Marsilio Ficino, Three Books on Life (De: Yates (1964) read De vita III chiefly as Hermetic magic, but that reading is challenged because Ficino titles the book as written among his Plotinus commentaries and Copenhaver (1984) sets it against scholastic philosophy and Ficino's worry about its orthodoxy. ([p. 151](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906831249ce014347d5b5c?page=151))
notes.Johannes Trithemius, Steganographia|||Re: Reeds (1998) reports solving the hidden ciphers in Book III and argues the Steganographia is the first book-length European treatment of cryptography, not a demonological treatise, so its spirit conjurations are not evidence of practised spirit magic.
notes.Johannes Trithemius, Antipalus maleficio: Reeds (1998) argues that Trithemius's Steganographia is cryptography rather than demonology, which bears on how this author's other works on spirits and magic should be read.

ideas.q: Is magic a mistake of thinking that every mind makes?

notes.J. G. Frazer, Folk-Lore in the Old Testa: Frazer explains the use of spittle in covenants as Contagious Magic, holding that spittle, being part of a man, is thought to give the spitter magical power over whoever swallows it, without saying here whether the habit is a mistake of every mind ([p. 120](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6a98bb1aec48f9ad103e3493?page=120)).
notes.Giambattista della Porta, Natural Magic: Porta treats sympathy and antipathy, the 'consent' and 'disagreement' of things arising from hidden properties, as the real ground on which the virtues of things are found, not as an error of thought ([p. 22](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=22)).
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books: Agrippa reports the magi's view that things act on each other by an innate power like the magnet on iron, and that through graded sympathy even intellectual and divine gifts can be received from above, a doctrine he sets out without treating it as a cognitive mistake ([p. 382](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=382)).
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, On the Vanit: Agrippa reports the magi's view that things act on each other by an innate power like the magnet on iron, and that through graded sympathy even intellectual and divine gifts can be received from above, a doctrine that bears on the question without being judged here as a universal error of mind ([p. 382](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=382)).
notes.Kenelm Digby, A Late Discourse on the Po: Digby presents the cure of James Howell's wound, through a bloodied garter put into a vitriol solution while Howell stood unaware across the room, as a working sympathetic cause rather than a mistake of thinking ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905b47aaa7f10ed4cfbadd?page=21)).
notes.E. B. Tylor, Primitive Culture|||Histori: Tylor makes the association of ideas the principal key to occult science, holding that man wrongly inverted connections found in experience and concluded that association in thought must involve similar connection in reality ([p. 120](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906a49d69de0e6980704da?page=120)).
notes.William Foster, Hoplocrisma-spongus: a S: Foster denies the sympathy explanation of the weapon-salve, arguing that since any substitute weapon, even a sallow stick, is said to work, there is no sympathy between the wound and the weapon, though he does not describe the belief as a habit of every mind ([p. 73](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69c812496c6f3cc53c847b2d?page=73)).

ideas.q: Is there a line between the natural and the supernatural?

notes.Iamblichus, On the Mysteries (De mysteri: Iamblichus ranks the pure soul as ὑπερφυής, living an unbegotten life outside every body and outside the nature divided around bodies, so he draws a line between bodily nature and what is above it ([p. 79](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69d13d751c2a66dc094b168d?page=79)).
notes.Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra gentiles II: Aquinas holds that a miracle is what God does beyond the order observed in things, ranks miracles by their distance from nature's capacity, and denies that any creature can work one ([p. 311](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69dbcc330f8c5edf20f477e9?page=311)) ([p. 312](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69dbcc330f8c5edf20f477e9?page=312)).
notes.Thomas Aquinas, On Evil (De malo) q. 16,: Aquinas marks the line with the phrases supra, contra and praeter naturam for God's miracles while demons can only apply bodily agents proportioned to the effect, and this line is drawn without needing the adjective supernaturalis ([p. 146](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69dbcc2a0f8c5edf20f46d51?page=146)) ([p. 339](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69dbcc290f8c5edf20f46beb?page=339)) ([p. 412](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69bd9c706120d54bd036eeb7?page=412)).
notes.Pietro Pomponazzi, On Incantations (De i: Pomponazzi explains reported wonders by natural powers without demons or angels, yet insists that the raising of Lazarus, the man born blind and the feeding of thousands cannot be reduced to any natural cause ([p. 165](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905f2040bc3a0478efaf14?page=165)) ([p. 247](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905f2040bc3a0478efaf14?page=247)) ([p. 111](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905f2040bc3a0478efaf14?page=111)).
notes.Giambattista della Porta, Natural Magic: Porta defines magic as nothing else but the survey of the whole course of Nature, leaving no separate region beyond nature for it to work in ([p. 16](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6953ea371479a63c11086267?page=16)).
notes.Joseph Glanvill, Saducismus triumphatus|: Glanvill judges the Tedworth disturbances to be something extraordinary that is usually called preternatural, so he sets them apart from ordinary nature, though the word itself ran in medical and marvel senses at once ([p. 286](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6952db2477f38f6761bc70c4?page=286)) ([p. 34](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69bd9f35f6d63c919747fc30?page=34)).
notes.David Hume, Of Miracles (An Enquiry conc: Hume defines a miracle as a violation of the laws of nature and holds that firm experience of those laws makes the proof against any miracle as entire as experience allows, with such reports abounding among ignorant and barbarous nations ([p. 158](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b64240535439aaa48939ab?page=158)) ([p. 163](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b64240535439aaa48939ab?page=163)).
notes.Alfred Russel Wallace, On Miracles and M: Wallace rejects Hume's definitions because they assume we know all the laws of nature, so that an invisible intelligent agent holding an apple in the air would not violate anything but would be one more agent at work ([p. 16](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6ab238b261b5fd3232b848c7?page=16)).
notes.Frank Podmore, The Naturalisation of the: Podmore treats the supernatural as a popular name for facts standing outside organised knowledge, whose claim is to be admitted within it, so the line is one of current knowledge that can be crossed ([p. 20](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6ab23d0c61b5fd3232b8d89a?page=20)).
notes.Max Weber, Economy and Society (Wirtscha: Weber puts supernatural in scare quotes and holds that the mark of religious development is that things count because they mean something, so the line that matters for magic is meaning and not nature versus beyond nature ([p. 310](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aea85d1cbf28a363a4f63c?page=310)) ([p. 250](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aea85d1cbf28a363a4f63c?page=250)).
notes.John Dee, Mathematicall Praeface to Eucl: Dee sorts beings into supernatural, natural and a middle kind of mathematical things, and he locates wonder-working in mathematical art and not in spirits ([p. 14](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=14)) ([p. 16](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=16)) ([p. 55](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=55)).
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books: Agrippa holds that mathematics is necessary to magic because works like nature's can be made by number, weight and measure, and that formal numbers carry greater hidden virtues than natural things, without stating where nature ends ([p. 217](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=217)) ([p. 220](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=220)).

ideas.q: Are number and mathematics above nature?

notes.Plato, Laws X–XI (on pharmakeia)|||Greek: The Epinomis holds that number is a gift of the god Heaven, that geometry is a divine wonder, and that the bond of number, diagram, harmony and stars shows all things full of gods ([p. 457](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69937734b0a84a57639630fa?page=457)) ([p. 474](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69937734b0a84a57639630fa?page=474)).
notes.Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Epistles (Rasāʾil), wit: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ treat geometry as a gate that leads students from sensible things to spiritual ones and to knowledge of the soul's substance ([p. 52](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69ef2f8272c1376fdf2af8f6?page=52)).
notes.Sefer Yetzirah (The Book of Formation)||: The Sefer Yetzirah has God form the world through thirty-two paths of wisdom, with number present as numberer, number and numbered before and within creation ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6970e3519b09d309d780a238?page=21)).
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books: Agrippa holds that number is the chief model in the Creator's mind, that formal numbers have greater virtue than natural things, and that material numbers act only as signs of intelligences above the world ([p. 220](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=220)) ([p. 265](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b642051c1c21a373889f10?page=265)) ([p. 217](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=217)).
notes.John Dee, Mathematicall Praeface to Eucl: Dee places mathematical things between the supernatural and the natural, and places number in the Creator and in angelic and human minds as well as in creatures, while holding that mathematical wonder-working needs no spirits ([p. 14](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=14)) ([p. 16](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=16)) ([p. 55](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=55)).
notes.John Dee, The Hieroglyphic Monad (Monas: Dee's Monas hieroglyphica reads the first representation of hidden natural things, and the beginning of existence itself, from the point, monad, line and circle, and claims a mathematical, magical, cabalistic and anagogic reading at once ([p. 23](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6952d04f77f38f6761bc4ee2?page=23)).
notes.Athanasius Kircher, Arithmologia|||Renai: Kircher holds that arithmetic and geometry have pure, demonstrable reasons and that the natural efficacy ascribed to magic numbers and figures is superstition, without saying where number stands relative to nature ([p. 81](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af0a0a4c57359b8d2d0f49?page=81)).
notes.Jacques Gaffarel, Unheard-of Curiosities: Gaffarel treats number symbolism as a store of curious examples, such as twenty as the number of sadness, and sends the reader to Bongo for a thousand more without taking a position on whether number is above nature ([p. 299](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/697a3055a3866af9498458ac?page=299)).

notes.Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles: Plutarch holds that daimones are of mixed nature with degrees of virtue and vice, so some are good, such as Hesiod's holy daimones and Plato's interpreting kind, while others are bad, such as the sullen natures behind grim festivals and the savage rites ascribed to 'some bad Daemons'. ([p. 108](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=108)) ([p. 109](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=109)) ([p. 108](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=108)) ([p. 41](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=41))
notes.Plato, Laws X–XI (on pharmakeia)|||Greek: The Epinomis treats the aerial daimones as a middle race worthy of prayer who love the good and hate the very wicked. ([p. 467](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69937734b0a84a57639630fa?page=467))
notes.Balthasar Bekker, The World Bewitched (D: Bekker argues that Scripture uses the name Daimones only for what exists in heathen imagination, not for real beings, so the question of their goodness does not arise. ([p. 557](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b176971643b0f241bd0349?page=557))
notes.Apuleius, On the God of Socrates (De deo: Apuleius holds that daemones are mediating, passible, aerial and eternal beings, among them the peaceful Lar who guards descendants and the good desire or Genius that is a good daemon, though a restless Larva harms the wicked. ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990633bef12272ffdc90769?page=21)) ([p. 17](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990633bef12272ffdc90769?page=17)) ([p. 22](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990633bef12272ffdc90769?page=22))
notes.Apuleius, Apology (De magia)|||Roman: Apuleius, in the Apology, bears on the question only through his account of daemones as intermediate beings who share human passions and can be swayed by gifts and prayers, without ruling on their goodness here. ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990633bef12272ffdc90769?page=21))
notes.Apuleius, Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass): Apuleius, in the Metamorphoses, bears on the question only through his account of daemones as intermediate beings who share human passions and can be swayed by gifts and prayers, without ruling on their goodness here. ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990633bef12272ffdc90769?page=21))
notes.Iamblichus, On the Mysteries (De mysteri: Iamblichus ranks daimones as one order in a hierarchy of higher kinds, serving the angels and served by heroes, and treats the rank as a place in the order rather than a moral class. ([p. 87](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69d13fe01c2a66dc094b1a6b?page=87))
notes.Porphyry, On Abstinence (De abstinentia): Porphyry blames evil-working daimones for plagues, famines and earthquakes and for deceiving people about the gods, which shows that some daimones are evil without settling whether any are good. ([p. 213](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990616cef12272ffdc8d980?page=213)) ([p. 406](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af447846e13536d25887fe?page=406))
notes.Augustine, City of God VIII–X|||Early Ch: Augustine rules that daemones are never good, rejecting Apuleius's intermediaries as proud, envious and deceitful spirits, reserving the good ones for the name of angels, and reading their knowledge as lacking charity. ([p. 365](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af447846e13536d25887fe?page=365)) ([p. 406](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af447846e13536d25887fe?page=406)) ([p. 407](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af447846e13536d25887fe?page=407)) ([p. 406](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af447846e13536d25887fe?page=406)) ([p. 372](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af447846e13536d25887fe?page=372))
notes.Marsilio Ficino, Three Books on Life (De: Ficino reports that a person's Daemon depends on the lord of the birth chart and that the ancients called the one descending from the eleventh house or an angle of the sky the 'good Daemon'. ([p. 167](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69dbc9fe1040d1d5e20a8528?page=167))
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books: Agrippa gives every person three good daemons as guardians, assigned by God, while also reporting that some theologians rank evil demons in nine degrees against the angelic orders. ([p. 483](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=483)) ([p. 258](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e11261c58d63664ecb5?page=258)) ([p. 333](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e1c768235dc6598c56a?page=333))
notes.Jean Bodin, On the Demon-Mania of Witche: Bodin attacks Weyer for appending to his book an index of a diabolical monarchy of 72 princes and millions of devils with their uses for invocation, and bears on the question only as a critic of such catalogues. ([p. 462](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905e022fd6a039938a0803?page=462))
notes.Johann Weyer, On the Tricks of Demons (D: Weyer's De praestigiis carried an appended index of a diabolical monarchy of 72 princes and millions of devils with their properties, which concerns evil spirits and does not address whether a daimon can be good. ([p. 462](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905e022fd6a039938a0803?page=462))
notes.Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcr: Scot catalogues devils and spirits by rank and command, as in Marbas the president who rules thirty-six legions, and so deals with ranked infernal spirits without asking whether a daimon can be good. ([p. 258](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6952310fab34727b1f0448a1?page=258))
notes.Mahāmāyūrī, the Great Peacock Spell-Quee: The Peacock Queen dhāraṇī names yakṣas as local deities with great armies under Vaiśravaṇa, protectors to be invoked and not demons. ([p. 22](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69f1343c365e3fcae574dff3?page=22))

ideas.q: Can music and sound work on the soul and on things?

notes.Marsilio Ficino, Three Books on Life (De: Ficino holds that a song conceived with the right virtue, timing and intention is another spirit, made solar, which acts on the singer and those nearby and can cure diseases of mind and body, as fascination acts through the eyes ([p. 159](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69dbc9fe1040d1d5e20a8528?page=159))
notes.Iamblichus, On the Mysteries (De mysteri: Iamblichus holds that music's natural power over the passions does not explain divine possession, and that cymbals and drums bring ecstasy because those sounds and songs are consecrated to particular gods, whose affinity makes them present at once ([p. 113](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69d13b3e1c2a66dc094b151a?page=113))
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books: Agrippa holds that harmony works wonders, citing Orpheus, David and the cure of Apulians bitten by the phalangium, and that antipathy acts through vocal harmony as well as touch, as in the wolfskin drum that silences a sheepskin one ([p. 284](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e15261c58d63664f304?page=284)) ([p. 280](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e78768235dc65993b9f?page=280))
notes.Iamblichus, On the Pythagorean Life|||He: Iamblichus's Pythagorean Life records Pythagoras's marvels, such as taming a bear by stroking, stopping an ox with a whisper, calming winds and waves, and bilocation, but nothing on it says that music or sound acts on spirits or things ([p. 71](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6955770557e3b773024f2d40?page=71)) ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69a956cd65ddd05bbcd3d083?page=21))
notes.Giambattista della Porta, Natural Magic: Porta reports that Apulians bitten by the tarantula sing, weep, rave and dance, and are restored by musical melodies that soften the spirit ([p. 193](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695258d1ab34727b1f045aed?page=193))
notes.Athanasius Kircher, The Magnet (Magnes,: Kircher presents music as the cure for tarantula poison, printing a map of Apulia with a tune called the Antidote of the Tarantula and the motto that music alone remains the medicine, and notes that the Tarantines name their specific melodies the tarantella ([p. 621](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b6a35d080b19f98fd19dd2?page=621))
notes.Athanasius Kircher, Musurgia universalis: Kircher treats the magic of consonance and dissonance as a natural magic, and holds that tarantism is cured by matching the instrument to the patient's complexion, with drums and trumpets for a cold slow temper and cithara, lute or harpsichord for mobile spirits ([p. 971](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b69ddb080b19f98fd0cec1?page=971)) ([p. 180](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51ed5c35d928cea4efe76?page=180))
notes.Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, The Book of Secr: The pseudo-Albertine secrets hold that a drum of wolfskin silences one of sheepskin, an antipathy working through sound ([p. 280](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e78768235dc65993b9f?page=280))
notes.Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, The Marvels of t: The pseudo-Albertine Marvels of the World carries the secret that a wolfskin drum silences a sheepskin one, an antipathy working through sound ([p. 280](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e78768235dc65993b9f?page=280))
notes.Albertus Magnus, On Minerals (De mineral: Albertus in De mineralibus treats the images and seals of stones as a part of necromancy subordinate to astronomy, and holds that figures in stones are sometimes made by nature, but he says nothing here about music or sound ([p. 56](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af21d4f98f6eff774cb8bf?page=56))
notes.Tommaso Campanella, On the Sense of Thin: Campanella holds that a sheepskin drum, especially from a sheep once terrified by a wolf, breaks when a wolfskin drum is beaten, because the passion sleeping in the skin is renewed by remembrance, and that magic has gained much business from such residual sense ([p. 327](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990652d726f64800c109dae?page=327))
notes.Giordano Bruno, On Magic (De magia)|||Re: Bruno explains the wolf-drum report by the spirit remaining in the dead skin mastering the sheep's spirit through antipathy, but says he has not tested it and suggests an ass-skin drum might win merely by its greater thickness ([p. 513](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905e232fd6a039938a1235?page=513))
notes.Giordano Bruno, On Bonds in General (De: On Bonds in General bears on the question only through Bruno's treatment of the wolf-drum report in De magia, where he offers a spirit-and-antipathy explanation but leaves it untested and allows a plain thickness explanation ([p. 513](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905e232fd6a039938a1235?page=513))
notes.Gaspar Schott, Universal Magic of Nature: Schott holds that an untouched unison string sounds by sympathy, through similar undulations of the air between alike-tensioned strings, and takes up how David's cithara healed Saul, judging that the Devil possessed Saul inwardly rather than accepting a purely medical reading ([p. 225](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b6b0fa96dc15d4a16cfb67?page=225)) ([p. 272](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b6b0fa96dc15d4a16cfb67?page=272))
notes.Tommaso Campanella, On Escaping Astral F: Campanella prescribes Jovial and Venereal music, within a rite of scents, fires, lights and torches, to break the malice of the air during an eclipse ([p. 246](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6991ed238bec46532eb4a262?page=246))
notes.Speculum astronomiae|||Medieval Latin: The Speculum astronomiae rejects images worked by fumigations and invocations and the exorcism of spirits by name, and sets apart astronomical images that work by their own nature under the heavens, without addressing music or sound ([p. 46](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=46)) ([p. 47](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=47)) ([p. 50](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=50))
notes.Lynn Thorndike, A History of Magic and E: Thorndike reports that Albertus condemns magic virtues worked by invocations and suffumigations as apostasy and holds that magical feats are natural forces hastened by demons and stars, with nothing on music or sound ([p. 566](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=566))
notes.Le Petit Albert (Secrets of Natural and: The Petit Albert offers cosmetics, household recipes and a sympathetic compass for writing to a distant friend, while its own warning calls diabolical invocations vain, and it makes no claim about music or sound ([p. 193](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695935a27d14807348773858?page=193)) ([p. 9](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695935a27d14807348773858?page=9))
notes.Gabriel Naudé, Apology for Great Men Acc: Naudé refutes planetary-image speaking heads and derives the legend of Albertus's metal Androides from the Hebrew teraphim, and treats the magus label as an accuser's smear, without addressing music or sound ([p. 269](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69c879e06c6f3cc53c858579?page=269)) ([p. 311](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699201597c226bdd25f989ad?page=311))
notes.Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies I: Hippolytus attacks those who divine the future by Pythagorean reckoning of numbers, elements and names, and says the heresiarchs borrowed the Pythagorean method of speaking in symbols, with nothing on music or sound ([p. 93](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69ac9bb999d9a0170d090d1e?page=93)) ([p. 922](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69a99ce86c7545e2236e12de?page=922))
notes.Pliny the Elder, Natural History XXX (th: Pliny says Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus and Plato sailed abroad to learn magic and on returning preached it and held it among their secrets, which places magic in the philosophers' lineage without saying anything about sound or music. ([p. 242](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b00f46f0043345da7679a6?page=242))
notes.Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcr: Scot repeats Pliny's list of Plato, Pythagoras, Empedocles and Democritus as travellers who learned natural magic, which he separates from witchcraft, and he says nothing here about music or sound acting on anything. ([p. 192](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6952310fab34727b1f0448a1?page=192))
notes.Johann Reuchlin, On the Art of Kabbalah: Reuchlin presents Pythagoras as drawing his philosophy from the Cabalists and has Philolaus call him a Cabalist, tracing a lineage of doctrine without addressing the power of music or sound. ([p. 714](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6974b642457dd8909910b9e5?page=714)) ([p. 53](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e359a81ef7feb3d1a02?page=53))
notes.Hygromanteia (Magical Treatise of Solomo: The Hygromanteia tradition, as published in the Anecdota atheniensia, includes a number-pair method of predicting marital harmony that its editor links to Pythagorean arithmetic onomatomancy, which is about numbers and names rather than sound. ([p. 149](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6a357f112aadc65cf0908511?page=149))
notes.John Wilkins, Mathematicall Magick|||Nat: Wilkins treats magic as mechanical geometry and automata, and he rejects as absurd the claim that articulate sounds could be shut up to make a speaking head, but he does not discuss music working on the soul or on things. ([p. 15](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=15)) ([p. 20](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=20)) ([p. 29](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=29)) ([p. 219](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=219)) ([p. 205](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=205)) ([p. 27](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=27))
notes.John Dee, Mathematicall Praeface to Eucl: Dee defends mathematical wonders such as self-moving works and the speaking brazen head as explicable by perspective and art, and denies that he is a conjurer of spirits, without claiming that music or sound acts on the soul or on things. ([p. 57](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=57)) ([p. 56](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=56))
notes.Edmond Doutté, Magic and Religion in Nor: Doutté gives the North African wafq, a numerical magic square whose 4x4 form matches the table of Jupiter that Agrippa prints, so his work bears on number magic and not on sound. ([p. 299](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=299))
notes.Eberhard David Hauber, Bibliotheca acta: Hauber reports that Naudé coined the word 'Androide' for Albertus's speaking image, which concerns the history of a term for a talking automaton and not any power of music or sound. ([p. 905](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906a08d69de0e69806f201?page=905))
notes.Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles: Plutarch explains oracular inspiration as a proportion between the imaginative part of the soul and the prophetic exhalation, and attributes the decline of oracles partly to the depopulation of Greece, without saying that music or sound moves the soul. ([p. 34](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=34)) ([p. 84](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=84))
notes.Isidore of Seville, Etymologies VIII.9 (: Isidore classifies divination by the four elements, citing Varro, and says the astrologers' nativity-casting was permitted only until the Gospel, with nothing on music or sound acting on spirits or things. ([p. 329](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af2339285bd73604373fd4?page=329)) ([p. 330](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af2339285bd73604373fd4?page=330))
notes.Pseudo-Agrippa, Fourth Book of Occult Ph: The geomancy printed with the pseudo-Agrippan Fourth Book maps the generated figures onto the houses of heaven, a divinatory scheme that does not address music or sound. ([p. 45](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695592397bd6d2cd1d619e4b?page=45))
notes.Peter Binsfeld, Treatise on the Confessi: Binsfeld reports that, following Aristotle, chiromancy is approved as a natural science and physiognomy is referred to the doctors, which bears on which divinations count as natural and not on the power of sound. ([p. 458](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699052368d19cbc90d9d57cf?page=458))

ideas.q: Can the future be known by signs?

notes.Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies I: Hippolytus attacks those who heed Pythagorean reckoning to divine the future by numbers, elements and names, and treats the practice as a heresiarch borrowing rather than a sound way of knowing what is coming ([p. 93](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69ac9bb999d9a0170d090d1e?page=93)).
notes.Iamblichus, On the Pythagorean Life|||He: Iamblichus says Pythagoras taught Abaris foreknowledge through numbers in place of divination by sacrifice, and Porphyry credits Pythagoras with predicting earthquakes ([p. 120](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69c88efc6c6f3cc53c85b25e?page=120)) ([p. 21](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69a956cd65ddd05bbcd3d083?page=21)).
notes.Plutarch, On the Obsolescence of Oracles: Plutarch holds that oracular prophecy is real and has a physical cause, a proportion between the soul's imaginative part and the prophetic exhalation, so it fails when that proportion fails or when a place is depopulated ([p. 84](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=84)) ([p. 34](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6992d67c46b85e738a0c5dde?page=34)).
notes.Isidore of Seville, Etymologies VIII.9 (: Isidore sorts divination by the four elements into geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy and pyromancy, and holds that reading nativities from the twelve signs was permitted until the Gospel and forbidden after Christ, which settles its licitness but not whether it works ([p. 329](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af2339285bd73604373fd4?page=329)) ([p. 330](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af2339285bd73604373fd4?page=330)).
notes.Peter Binsfeld, Treatise on the Confessi: Binsfeld, following Aristotle, approves chiromancy on the lines of the hands as a natural science and refers physiognomy to the doctors ([p. 458](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699052368d19cbc90d9d57cf?page=458)).
notes.Pseudo-Agrippa, Fourth Book of Occult Ph: The English geomancy printed with the Fourth Book gives a working method that maps the eight generated figures onto the houses of heaven, the four Mothers as the first four houses and the four Daughters as the next four ([p. 45](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695592397bd6d2cd1d619e4b?page=45)).
notes.Speculum astronomiae|||Medieval Latin: The Speculum astronomiae rejects the fumigation-and-invocation mode of images as the worst idolatry and the spirit-exorcising mode as suspect, and sets apart astronomical images that work by their own nature as constrained by the heavens, which is about making effects rather than reading the future ([p. 46](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=46)) ([p. 47](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=47)) ([p. 50](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=50)).
notes.Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, The Book of Secr: This work rests on the Speculum's three modes of images and Albertus's treatment of stone images, which he calls a part of necromancy yet allows that nature sometimes makes figures in stones and that some are frauds, and none of this addresses knowing the future by signs ([p. 46](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=46)) ([p. 47](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=47)) ([p. 50](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=50)) ([p. 56](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af21d4f98f6eff774cb8bf?page=56)) ([p. 58](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af21d4f98f6eff774cb8bf?page=58)).
notes.Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, The Marvels of t: This work rests on the Speculum's three modes of images and Albertus's treatment of stone images, which he calls a part of necromancy yet allows that nature sometimes makes figures in stones and that some are frauds, and none of this addresses knowing the future by signs ([p. 46](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=46)) ([p. 47](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=47)) ([p. 50](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906ed28a353648e1ed04da?page=50)) ([p. 56](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af21d4f98f6eff774cb8bf?page=56)) ([p. 58](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af21d4f98f6eff774cb8bf?page=58)).
notes.Albertus Magnus, On Minerals (De mineral: Albertus calls the doctrine of images and seals of stones a part of necromancy subalternated to astronomy, holds that nature sometimes paints figures in stones, and warns that others are alchemical frauds, all without addressing foreknowledge by signs ([p. 56](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af21d4f98f6eff774cb8bf?page=56)) ([p. 58](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69af21d4f98f6eff774cb8bf?page=58)).
notes.Lynn Thorndike, A History of Magic and E: Thorndike reports that Albertus condemns magic virtues as evil and apostasy and explains magical feats as natural forces aided by demons and stars, and he lists manuscripts of the Sphere of Pythagoras and the Circle of Petosiris as spheres of life and death, without himself judging whether signs reveal the future ([p. 566](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699069252f82e0fda48046c3?page=566)) ([p. 739](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699069212f82e0fda4804270?page=739)).
notes.Le Petit Albert (Secrets of Natural and: The Petit Albert, in its own Warning, calls marvelous secrets, chiromancy and diabolical invocations vain propositions, even as it offers household recipes and a sympathetic dial for writing to a distant friend ([p. 9](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695935a27d14807348773858?page=9)) ([p. 193](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695935a27d14807348773858?page=193)).
notes.Gabriel Naudé, Apology for Great Men Acc: Naudé refutes the legend that Albertus cast a speaking metal Androides under constellations, derives it from the Hebrew teraphim, and mocks the works attributed to Albert and the charge of magic against the philosophers, without taking up reading the future by signs ([p. 269](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69c879e06c6f3cc53c858579?page=269)) ([p. 101](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6974b63b19126e775cf6d7cb?page=101)) ([p. 311](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/699201597c226bdd25f989ad?page=311)) ([p. 269](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69c879e06c6f3cc53c858579?page=269)).
notes.Pliny the Elder, Natural History XXX (th: Pliny says Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus and Plato sailed in exile to learn magic and on returning preached it and kept it among their secrets, which concerns the history of magic and not whether signs reveal the future.
notes.Reginald Scot, The Discoverie of Witchcr: Scot repeats Pliny's list of philosophers who travelled to learn natural magic, which he distinguishes from witchcraft, and says nothing about knowing the future by signs ([p. 192](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6952310fab34727b1f0448a1?page=192)).
notes.Johann Reuchlin, On the Art of Kabbalah: Reuchlin presents Kabbalah as a symbolic philosophy from which Pythagoras drew his doctrine and promises a Pythagoras reborn, without addressing foreknowledge by signs ([p. 714](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6974b642457dd8909910b9e5?page=714)) ([p. 53](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e359a81ef7feb3d1a02?page=53)).
notes.Hygromanteia (Magical Treatise of Solomo: The Greek manuscript tradition gives a method of predicting marital harmony from number pairs, which its editor links to the arithmetic onomatomancy Hippolytus attributes to the Pythagoreans ([p. 149](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6a357f112aadc65cf0908511?page=149)).
notes.Marsilio Ficino, Three Books on Life (De: Ficino holds that a song conceived with the right virtue, timing and intention is another spirit beside the singer's own, able to act on those nearby and to cure diseases of mind and body, which concerns music's effects and not foreknowledge ([p. 159](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69dbc9fe1040d1d5e20a8528?page=159)).
notes.Iamblichus, On the Mysteries (De mysteri: Iamblichus answers Porphyry that music's natural power over the passions does not explain divine possession, which comes because sounds and songs are consecrated to particular gods who are made present by their affinity, so the passage bears on how inspiration arises and not on reading signs ([p. 113](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69d13b3e1c2a66dc094b151a?page=113)).
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books: Agrippa treats musical wonders, antipathy acting in sound, mathematical automata and the planetary number tables as working through natural, mathematical and divine proportion, and the work does not itself claim that these signs disclose the future ([p. 284](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e15261c58d63664f304?page=284)) ([p. 280](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51e78768235dc65993b9f?page=280)) ([p. 217](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=217)) ([p. 292](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=292)) ([p. 299](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=299)).
notes.Tommaso Campanella, On the Sense of Thin: Campanella holds that a sheepskin drum tears when a wolfskin drum is beaten because the skin keeps a sleeping passion renewed by remembrance, and says magic has gained much business from such residual sense, without treating it as a way to read the future ([p. 327](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990652d726f64800c109dae?page=327)).
notes.Giordano Bruno, On Magic (De magia)|||Re: Bruno explains the wolf-drum report by the spirit left in the dead skin overpowering the sheep's spirit through antipathy, admits he has not tested it, and offers a thickness explanation for an ass-skin drum, with nothing on foretelling ([p. 513](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905e232fd6a039938a1235?page=513)).
notes.Giordano Bruno, On Bonds in General (De: The only material here is Bruno's account in De magia of the wolf-drum report as spirit in dead skin acting by antipathy, which he has not tested, and it does not bear on knowing the future by signs ([p. 513](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905e232fd6a039938a1235?page=513)).
notes.Gaspar Schott, Universal Magic of Nature: Schott treats sympathy between untouched strings, the cure of Saul by David's cithara, and Albertus's speaking head as questions of natural or demonic cause, and does not address reading the future from signs ([p. 225](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b6b0fa96dc15d4a16cfb67?page=225)) ([p. 272](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b6b0fa96dc15d4a16cfb67?page=272)) ([p. 197](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b6b0fa96dc15d4a16cfb67?page=197)).
notes.Athanasius Kircher, Musurgia universalis: Kircher presents the magic of consonance and dissonance as natural magic that awakens wonderful sounds and fits the instrument to the patient's complexion, a matter of healing and not of foretelling ([p. 180](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b51ed5c35d928cea4efe76?page=180)) ([p. 971](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b69ddb080b19f98fd0cec1?page=971)).
notes.Athanasius Kircher, The Magnet (Magnes,: Kircher prints a tarantula antidote tune and says music alone is the medicine for the poison, which concerns cure by music and not knowledge of the future ([p. 621](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69b6a35d080b19f98fd19dd2?page=621)).
notes.Giambattista della Porta, Natural Magic: Porta reports that Apulians bitten by the tarantula are restored by melodies that soften the spirit, and gives a way to lure and powder the spider, with no claim about reading the future ([p. 193](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/695258d1ab34727b1f045aed?page=193)).
notes.Tommaso Campanella, On Escaping Astral F: Campanella prescribes a rite of scents, fires, lights and Jovial and Venereal music to break the malice of an eclipse and draw benefic planets, so he treats the heavens as a force to be countered and does not say whether their signs reveal the future ([p. 246](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6991ed238bec46532eb4a262?page=246)).
notes.John Wilkins, Mathematicall Magick|||Nat: Wilkins presents Mathematicall Magick as wonders done by mechanical geometry, which vulgar opinion mistakes for magic, and he explains automata such as Archytas's dove and the brazen heads by mechanism, with no bearing on divination ([p. 15](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=15)) ([p. 20](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=20)) ([p. 29](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=29)) ([p. 219](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=219)) ([p. 205](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=205)) ([p. 27](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe60c0472fef6455a8f3?page=27)).
notes.John Dee, Mathematicall Praeface to Eucl: Dee denies that studying creatures' wonderful virtues to glorify God makes one a conjurer of spirits, and says perspective can explain works wrongly judged above nature, such as Albertus's speaking brazen head, without taking up foretelling ([p. 57](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=57)) ([p. 56](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69aebe88a103e42dc94145ad?page=56)).
notes.Edmond Doutté, Magic and Religion in Nor: Doutté gives the North African wafq, a magic square with constant sum 34, which is the same square Agrippa prints as the table of Jupiter, and the evidence does not say it is used to read the future ([p. 299](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/698420e1f1fb376a3d58061c?page=299)).
notes.Eberhard David Hauber, Bibliotheca acta: Hauber reports that Naudé coined the word Androide for Albertus's speaking image, a point of vocabulary with nothing on knowing the future by signs ([p. 905](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69906a08d69de0e69806f201?page=905)).

ideas.q: Can thought alone change the world, as New Thought taught?
ideas.t: New Thought and the law of attraction

notes.Franz Anton Mesmer, Mémoire sur la décou: Mesmer holds that the influence between bodies is carried by a universal physical fluid obeying mechanical laws, so the agent is physics and not thought. ([p. 86](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6990580e1729589044135366?page=86))
notes.Marquis de Puységur, Mémoires on Animal: Puységur holds that the whole doctrine comes down to the operator's belief in a power within himself and the will to use it, and he has his patient Victor prescribe his own treatment in the magnetic state. ([p. 157](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6991bd4770254d38471e39e6?page=157)) ([p. 233](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905f1440bc3a0478efa351?page=233))
notes.James Braid, Magic, Witchcraft, Animal M: Braid holds that the effects credited to magic and animal magnetism are real but come from suggestion working on an imaginative, docile subject, so mind moves mind while no magical agent exists. ([p. 74](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6991bd5870254d38471e4c64?page=74))
notes.Phineas P. Quimby, The Quimby Manuscript: Quimby holds that disease is a belief and that the healer's explanation of the error is the cure, after he dropped the magnetic-current idea because it explained nothing. ([p. 53](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905c87aaa7f10ed4cfbefb?page=53)) ([p. 155](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905c87aaa7f10ed4cfbefb?page=155))
notes.Mary Baker Eddy, Science and Health|||Ne: Eddy holds that the cause of all disease is mental, a mortal fear or mistaken belief, that patients recover once the belief goes, and that animal magnetism is error and no fluid exists. ([p. 397](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6a5837d96701425b993051ba?page=397)) ([p. 504](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6a5837d96701425b993051ba?page=504))
notes.Warren Felt Evans, The Mental Cure|||New: Evans holds that mesmerism and its kin are one principle, the action of mind upon mind, and that inharmonious mental states ultimate themselves in matching bodily conditions through Swedenborgian correspondence. ([p. 256](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905c8baaa7f10ed4cfc0d7?page=256)) ([p. 103](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69905c8baaa7f10ed4cfc0d7?page=103))
notes.Warren Felt Evans, Esoteric Christianity: Evans grounds mental healing in a law of sympathy running through nature, the same law on which he says Proclus's ancient magic rested, and he appeals to the Hermetic philosophers for the power of the receptive mind. ([p. 13](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6ab22d844ac37d55a212de96?page=13)) ([p. 24](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6ab22d844ac37d55a212de96?page=24))
notes.Asclepius (the Latin Hermetic dialogue)|: The ancient priests, as Proclus reports, founded sacred science on the sympathy of natural things with one another and with hidden powers, which is the older law that later teachers recast as attraction by thought. ([p. 457](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/68fb0dc412055a03a58d3281?page=457))
notes.Proclus, On the Hieratic Art (De sacrifi: Proclus says the ancient priests founded their sacred science on the kinship and sympathy of natural things with one another and with hidden powers, finding all things in all things, and he does not make thought the cause. ([p. 457](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/68fb0dc412055a03a58d3281?page=457))
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, Three Books: Agrippa reports the magi's view that things act on each other by an innate power like the magnet on iron, and that graded sympathy lets intellectual and divine gifts be received from above. ([p. 382](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=382))
notes.Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, On the Vanit: Agrippa reports the magi's view that things act on each other by innate sympathy like the magnet on iron, with divine gifts descending through it according to Iamblichus, Proclus and Synesius. ([p. 382](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/69bd9ca46120d54bd037001f?page=382))
notes.Emma Curtis Hopkins, High Mysticism|||Ne: Hopkins calls her teaching on faith the Magia Jesu Christi and holds that the practitioner's own word is magia. ([p. 51](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6ab235a74ac37d55a213ca14?page=51))
notes.Prentice Mulford, Your Forces, and How t: Mulford holds that mind is magnetic because it attracts whatever thought it fixes on, and that qualities like patience or courage are real elements one draws by demanding them. ([p. 43](https://sourcelibrary.org/book/6a3e6624629ea5110b4c8b24?page=43))

Wattles, The Science of Getti: Wattles holds that a thinking stuff fills the universe and that a thought held in it produces the thing thought of, on a monistic footing he calls Hindu in origin. links.b: Augustine, City of God VIII–X|||Early Christian & Monastic

links.a: Asclepius (the Latin Hermetic dialogue)|||Hermetic & Gnostic
links.b: Marsilio Ficino, Three Books on Life (De vita libri tres)|||Renaissance & Early Modern Europe
links.n: Ficino, following Aquinas, judges that speaking statues, if they ever spoke, spoke by daemons, not by the influence of the stars.

links.a: Porphyry, Letter to Anebo|||Hellenistic & Late Antique
links.b: Iamblichus, On the Mysteries (De mysteriis)|||Hellenistic & Late Antique
links.n: Iamblichus answers Porphyry's doubts about the rites: theurgy works by the rites themselves, not by thought.

links.a: Augustine, City of God VIII–X|||Early Christian & Monastic
links.b: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Oration on the Dignity of Man|||Renaissance & Early Modern Europe
links.n: Augustine makes goetia and theurgy one demonic art; Pico restores the Greek split, the demons' work, "execrable and monstrous", against magic as the perfection of natural philosophy.

links.b: Pietro Pomponazzi, On Incantations (De incantationibus)|||Renaissance & Early Modern Europe
links.n: Aquinas gives the works of magicians to demons; Pomponazzi sets out to explain the same wonders "without recourse to demons or angels".

links.b: Giambattista della Porta, Natural Magic (Magia naturalis)|||Natural Magic & Early Science
links.n: Both keep the wonders inside nature; Porta reports magic defined as "the practical part of natural Philosophy".

links.b: John Wilkins, Mathematicall Magick|||Natural Magic & Early Science
links.n: Agrippa's mathematical wonders (moving statues, Archytas's dove) come "with celestial influxes added"; Wilkins keeps the machines and calls them magic only in allusion to vulgar opinion.

links.b: Athanasius Kircher, Arithmologia|||Renaissance & Early Modern Europe

tested.how: Bruno explained the drum by the wolf's spirit left in the skin but said he had not tried it. Schott reports it.

verdict.title: Does “magic” translate?
verdict.text: Not as one neutral word. A reader checked the words for magic in 10 traditions on this map (Greek, Latin Christian, Renaissance learned, French and German, Hebrew, Arabic, Indic, Tibetan, Chinese and Japanese). None has one neutral word for what English now calls magic. In 7 of the 10 the words split into a licit and an illicit kind, by who does it, against whom and by what power; the Latin church refused the split and called all of it the demons' work, and in the Tibetan sources even the fierce rites are a sanctioned practice. Most of the words come down to us from the accuser: the jurist, the theologian or the state. Magic as one category of practice is a modern idea, put together after about 1750 by people who no longer believed it worked.
